Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: 'Shouting in Arabic' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless there is specific trauma detail indicating the stalker used Arabic; with the rest of the profile, this trigger appears overly specific and disconnected from the other stalking-related items.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same Memory node items describing fragmented, intrusive, partially inaccessible trauma memory ('extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'fragments appear suddenly without warning'). While not impossible, this is a direct enough tension within the node to question coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: Fear of losing control of anger and doing something terrible is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile, which centers on fear, mistrust, stranger threat, and life damage after stalking. It points toward a perpetration/harm-to-others concern not otherwise represented in Threat, Triggers, Memory, or strategies, making the formulation less coherent.

vignette:
Anna Weber is a 28-year-old elementary school teacher who came to treatment after more than a year of living as if danger were always just behind her. She described the beginning of it as a period when a man began appearing near her apartment, then outside the school where she worked, and later along the route she took home. At first she tried to explain it away. He stood too long across the street, showed up again a few days later, then again at dismissal time when children were being picked up and the sidewalk was crowded with parents. Over time his presence became harder to dismiss. What stayed with Anna most sharply was not a single dramatic scene but a series of moments that felt invasive and inescapable: turning and realizing he was behind her on the sidewalk, hearing heavy breathing close enough that she could tell it was directed toward her, sensing him matching her pace as the street around them suddenly seemed to empty out. Some parts of that period were fixed in her mind with painful precision-the sound of his breathing, the feeling of checking over her shoulder, the sight of him near the school gate-while other stretches were blank. She said she knew what happened, but when she tried to describe it aloud, her words disappeared and she was left shaking her head, frustrated by how little she could make herself say.

After she reported the stalking, contact with police did not bring the sense of safety she had expected. Instead, the sight of officers, police cars, or uniforms became charged in its own way, immediately returning her to those weeks of reporting, waiting, and still feeling exposed. She could be walking past a patrol car and feel her body tense before she had even consciously registered why. Since then, fragments of memory have broken into the present without warning. A sound, a patch of quiet, or the sensation that someone is walking just behind her can bring back a piece of it for a second or two-a breath at her shoulder, the certainty of being tracked-before it vanishes again, leaving her rattled and ashamed that she still cannot tell the story cleanly from beginning to end.

At school, where she once felt competent and relaxed, Anna now moves through the hallways with constant watchfulness. She notices footsteps behind her, pauses at classroom doors, checks the parking lot before walking to her car, and is acutely alert when the building goes unusually quiet after the students leave. Silence frightens her almost as much as noise. In those moments she feels sure something dangerous is about to happen, as if the absence of ordinary classroom sound means someone is there, waiting. If a parent she does not recognize approaches her too quickly after dismissal, she feels a surge of fear before she can assess the situation. Strangers in ordinary settings-at the grocery store, on the sidewalk, outside her building-do not feel neutral to her anymore. She has come to experience unfamiliar people as possible threats, and she watches them closely until she can leave.

These habits have narrowed her life. She asks her boyfriend to meet her after late school events rather than walk out alone. She changes routes, avoids staying in the classroom after dark, and has become noticeably guarded with colleagues and parents. She used to chat easily at pickup time; now she keeps conversations brief and scans the area while talking. Inside, she is certain that people cannot be trusted, because the world has already shown her how easily someone can cross into her life and remain there. She speaks as if the stalking divided her life into a before and after, and the after feels ruined to her. What frightened her most was not only what the man did, but the conviction that she must never stop being on guard. To let down her attention even briefly feels reckless.

By the time Anna sought help, she was exhausted by the force of her own fear and by the effort of containing it at work. The immediate reason for coming in was an incident after a faculty meeting: as the building emptied and the corridor fell silent, she heard heavy breathing behind her, spun around in panic, and found only another staff member hurrying past. She went home shaken, unable to explain to her boyfriend why such a small moment had undone her so completely. In session she said she was afraid this was now her permanent life-that teaching, walking home, hearing someone behind her, even seeing police, would always feel dangerous. At the same time, she said she wanted desperately to believe that she could stand in an ordinary quiet hallway again without feeling hunted.
